Reasons for
Judgment released on 20 July 2004

ACCESS TO CHILD — Form of order — Supervised
access — Grounds — Parental impasse — Supervised access is interim measure
reserved for resolving impasse over access that should evolve to more normal
access regime — It has distinct disadvantages such as (1) conveying message
that child’s safety cannot be otherwise entrusted to access parent (which in
this case, was pernicious message because evidence did not support conclusion
that father presented any sort of risk to child); (2) reducing access time
because it must accommodate access centre’s availability and hours of
operation; and (3) costing money — In this case, even though court ended
supervision about 2 years ago, mother wanted return to supervised access but
offered no evidence at trial to justify step backwards to renewed involvement
of supervised access centre — Mother’s request for supervised access dismissed.

ACCESS TO CHILD — Form of order — Supervised
access — Grounds — Risk of harm to child — Access to former child abuser —
Father’s interim access order included term prohibiting son’s unsupervised access
to paternal grandfather who, 10 years ago, pleaded guilty to charge of sexual
touching of his then 11-year-old daughter and who received suspended sentence
and probation — Grandfather had completed his probation and had had no criminal
record since then (or even prior to that offence) — Social worker with Office
of Children’s Lawyer recommended continued restriction on grandfather’s contact
with boy but could identify no “risk” specific to this boy and this grandfather
— Worker’s reliance on vague unaccredited dogma of “once labelled, forever
labelled” was speculation and conjecture but not evidence of likely risk to
child — Court could find no likelihood of risk to boy in his grandfather’s
unsupervised presence and rejected request for supervised access.

CIVIL PROCEDURE — Offers to settle — General
— When to file with court — During trial — In claim for joint custody where
court was examining level of co-operation that parties had demonstrated during
litigation, it paid particular attention to various interim agreements that
formed part of trial evidence — Court refused, however, mother’s invitation
also to examine offers to settle — Offers to settle cannot be examined during
trial and come before court only for purpose of decision of liability and quantum
of costs.

CUSTODY OF CHILD — Best interests of child —
Conduct of parties — Resistance to court process — Custodial mother who firmly
believed that child’s relationship with father had no value repeatedly ignored,
stalled or created impediments to implementation of string of access orders —
Mother effectively sabotaged order for investigation and report by Office of
Children’s Lawyer by withholding child from observational visit at father’s
home — When investigating social worker at Office of Children’s Lawyer sought
mother’s consent to speak with persons likely to have information for proposed
report, mother regarded overture as attack on her character and then set about
to attack worker’s competence and professionalism.

CUSTODY OF CHILD — Best interests of child —
Fostering ties to non-custodial parent — Evidence showed that mother’s
enthusiasm for cultivating relationship between father and child was, at best,
lukewarm and, at worst, irresponsible and mean-spirited — At start of case,
mother obtained
ex parte
order custody order on evidence that, at trial,
was shown to have no basis in truth — Despite string of court orders dealing
with father’s access, mother (with support of child’s maternal grandfather who
shared mother’s belief that child’s relationship with father had no value)
consistently ignored, stalled or created impediments to implementation of
court-ordered access — She failed to complete intake requirements at access
centre in timely manner — She then “discovered” problems in transporting child
to and from access centre and chose another centre that forced father to travel
longer distances on public transit — Court could not trust mother as sole
custodian of child and, despite difficulties in parents’ ability to co-operate,
it imposed joint custody to promote child’s best interests.

CUSTODY OF CHILD — Form of order — Joint
custody — Grounds — Court’s distrust of principal caregiver as sole custodian —
Evidence at trial showed that mother’s enthusiasm for cultivating relationship
between father and child was, at best, lukewarm and, at worst, irresponsible
and mean-spirited — Appeal courts have ruled that joint custody needs to be
predicated on high degree of co-operation between parents but this should not
preclude joint custody in situations where one parent deliberately provokes and
engineers discord in expectation of being rewarded with sole custody and
escaping any examination of source of and impetus for ongoing conflict — If
used carefully, joint custody within parallel parenting plan may promote
child’s best interests in cases where court finds that it would not serve
child’s best interests to entrust primary caregiver with sole decision-making
power — In this case, child’s bond with access father was strong, despite
mother’s efforts to frustrate it — Father’s plan of parenting time with child
was modest and built incrementally on regime currently in place — Unlike
mother, he had never sought to impair child’s relationship with mother and had
always respected child’s ties of affection with her and her family — He had always
been ready to work co-operatively with mother had been generous and flexible
with mother in access arrangements — Removal of sole decision-making power from
mother would ensure that decisions that previously caused disruption if
implemented would no longer feed mother’s needs and whims but would centre on
child’s needs and benefits — Joint custody ordered.

CUSTODY OF CHILD — General — Rights of
parent — Where parents separate — Parent with
de facto
or
de jure

custody has (1) no authority to deny child access to other parent or to dictate
terms of child’s access; and (2) no authority to withhold information from
other parent or to obstruct other parent’s inquiries about child’s well being
(such as child’s health, education and welfare) — Non-custodial parent’s rights
to access and information survive separation unless court order or agreement provides
otherwise.

CUSTODY OF CHILD — Interim custody — General
— Purpose of interim custody order — At best, interim order is temporary solution,
made on partial and untested evidence, for child’s ongoing care until outcome
of court case —
Ex parte
interim order is most temporary of interim
orders, resting on evidence not even exposed to challenge of other parent —
Such orders therefore are weak foundations on which to construct any argument
for continuity of care (
status quo
).

RESTRAINING ORDER — Grounds — Harassment,
molestation or annoyance — Evidence — Mother’s evidence for
ex parte

interim restraining order against father was exposed at trial as untruthful —
Her “fear” of recurrence of alleged spousal abuse was, at best, figment of her
imagination and, at worst, deliberate fabrication to hide her role in breakdown
of parents’ relationship and to portray father as unfit parent — Mother failed
to adduce any evidence of any abuse or threatening behaviour by father —
Instead, evidence revealed that she marketed her alleged “fear” as reason for
avoiding something that she did not want to do, such as complying with access orders
or sharing information about child with father — Allegation of abuse is not
proof of abuse and claim of fear is by itself no proof of good reason for that
fear — There had never been need for restraining order against father — Court
dismissed mother’s attempt to turn back clock on claim that should have been
discontinued long ago.

JUSTICE KATARYNYCH:—

1:     INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The child at the heart of this nine-day trial
is M.P.R.W., born on […] 1999 to the applicant and the respondent.

[
2
]

His mother’s application first came before
the court on 31 January 2001 in the wake of an
ex parte
motion brought
by her on 8 January 2001, seeking orders granting her sole custody, child
support, a restraining non-harassment order against the respondent, restricted
and supervised access between the child and father, including a term that she
be allowed to provide all food for the visits and spousal support.  At trial,
an additional claim was introduced into the case in the course of judicial case
management, for supervision of the child’s access to his paternal grandfather.

[
3
]

The father answered the application with
claims for access to the child, beginning with a supervised access, fair notice
of the child’s unavailability for access due, for example, to birthday parties
and religious observances, the lifting of the
ex parte
restraining order
made on 8 January 2001 so that the parents could communicate directly with each
other on matters related to the child’s health and well being, a mobility
restriction and a restriction on any change in the child’s name.  In the course
of judicial case management, he had replaced his access claim with one for a
joint custody, with his home as a secondary residence and the child’s
continuing to have his primary residence with the mother.

[
4
]

Judgment on the child support claim was
released on 13 July 2004.  This is the judgment on the remaining claims but for
the claim respecting costs.

[
5
]

●    the maternal

●    Ms. L.F., an

●    Children’s Lawyer

[
6
]

The documentary evidence at trial was
constituted by exhibits 1 to 40 inclusive.  When the evidentiary cases for each
party closed on 20 April 2004,
it was understood that certain documents, not yet admitted into evidence, would
be the subject of evidentiary rulings as part of this court’s consideration of

3:     THE LAW APPLIED IN THE ADJUDICATION

[
7

I have intentionally interwoven the law

4:     FINDINGS OF FACT

4.1:     On the Child M.P.R.W.

[
8
]

On the whole of the trial evidence, I made
the following findings of fact:

(a)    The applicant and
respondent are this child’s biological parents, born to them on [...] 1999.

(b)    He is their first and
only child.  Although not a planned baby, he was a welcomed one and to his
mother, her “miracle baby”.  He is dearly loved by both parents.

(c)    He was just 15 months
when this litigation began.  He will have his 5th birthday this upcoming
October.

(d)    This parental dispute
has consumed important years in his growth and development and the ability of
his father to be a meaningful part of that growth and development.

(e)    As between the two
parents, both before and after the parental separation at the end of December
2000, his mother has been his primary caregiver.

(f)    He has an interested and
responsible extended family on both sides of his heritage, although the
involvement of the paternal extended family in his life to date has not been as
extensive as that of the maternal extended family with whom he has resided
since August 2002.

(g)    Although born healthy at
38½ weeks gestation with a birth weight of 6 pounds, 3 ounces, and “top score”
Apgar readings, he was over the course of his infancy — on the uncontradicted
testimony of his mother and in her perception — “quite sickly”, susceptible to
“flu bugs” and ear infections, had difficulty adjusting to formula and was
ultimately found to be lactose intolerant.

(h)    When M.P.R.W. was
approximately three months old, his father was left alone with him for a time
and shook him briefly in frustration when he could not get him to stop crying.

(i)    On the uncontradicted
medical evidence constituted by the record of the Hospital for Sick Children
reflecting its investigation, including the clinical input of the hospital’s
specialized child abuse investigation team who examined the infant in the aftermath
of the shaking (exhibit 5), M.P.R.W. suffered no lasting harm from this brief
shaking.  He was not hospitalized then or at any later point in relation to
this incident.  No court proceeding was launched by a children’s aid society to
have the child found to be a child in need of protection in his parents’ care.
The father was not prosecuted in the criminal courts.  It did not prompt a
lasting separation of the parents.  On the mother’s own evidence, she and the
baby stayed at her parents’ residence temporarily and then returned to the
family home, and both parents responded to the incident through requirements on
both of them set out in a voluntary service agreement with the society (exhibit
25).

(j)    On the uncontradicted
evidence of the mother, M.P.R.W. has been delayed in some aspects of his
development; not crawling until 11 months of age, not walking until 18 months
of age and, at the time of trial, was not yet managing control of his bowels in
his day-care facility.

(k)    On the uncontradicted
evidence of his mother, he has been subjected to a number of clinical
investigations and interventions over the course of this litigation, all
initiated by the mother’s concerns about him, including services of both the
Hincks-Dellcrest Centre in Toronto sometime before his second birthday (the
evidence is unclear on this point) until the summer of 2002 and more recently,
the Clarke Institute (now the Centre for Mental Health and Addiction) in relation
to behavioural problems.

(l)    At the close of the
trial, he was awaiting further clinical investigations of him, those also
initiated by the mother’s concern about him — specifically, neurological examinations
and speech therapy assessment.

(m)    In his mother’s
experience of him, he has been an emotionally fragile child — “a mess” — in the
aftermath of the parental separation, plagued with “very violent nightmares”,
easily startled and seemingly “afraid of being punished all the time”.  As time
went on, his aggression toward others and toward himself and his “clingy”
behaviour prompted his mother’s outreach to the Hincks Dellcrest Centre for
some assistance with him.

(n)    At the close of the
trial, M.P.R.W. was still, in his mother’s eyes, a fragile and immature child,
one having “a lot of issues”, “overly sensitive”, “very sucky in a lot of ways”
and “a lot more like a three year old than five year old, if not even younger”.

(o)    After the parental
separation in late December 2000 and until M.P.R.W. moved with his mother to
the home of his maternal grandparents in August 2002, there had been a lot of
“to and fro” for him.  When his mother left the family home with him on 21
December 2000,some two months after his first birthday, it was an abrupt uprooting,
with no involvement of his father in easing the transition for him.  He went
with his mother to stay a few days in a cousin’s home, then further relocated
with his mother to the home of her parents, then moved back to his family home,
since his father had vacated it, as his mother had wished, and then to a less
expensive unit in the same student housing complex before he was finally moved
to the home of his maternal grandparents.

(p)    M.P.R.W. lost contact
with his father for a period of some eight months after the parental separation
and was then expected to make a rapid adjustment to the re-entry of his father
to his life in circumstances where the mother saw no real value in that reunion
and did little to support it.

(q)    M.P.R.W. was in the care
of a mother who was herself very fragile in the aftermath of the separation,
“very insecure” at that time, as she herself described her feelings, in a
“state of fear like M.P.R.W.”, “kind of messed up” and lacking confidence in
her ability to manage without the father’s assistance.

(r)    M.P.R.W. had to adjust
to the parenting style of a number of caregivers in the aftermath of the
separation.  On the uncontradicted evidence of his mother, she has changed
day-care providers a number of times — in one instance because of a “personality
clash” between her and the provider; in another instance, because the care
provider decided to withdraw her service after being contacted by the Office of
the Children’s Lawyer; in yet another instance, because she did not want the
day care knowing about the parental dispute and the court had recently ordered
the father to begin his access on alternate Fridays by collecting the child
from the day care.

(s)    Although the maternal
grandfather echoed the mother’s perceptions about the child’s behaviour
problems, the maternal grandmother, herself a teacher of young children, made
no mention of any extraordinary difficulty in her experience of this grandson.

(t)    In his father’s
experience of him and the experience of others in the extended paternal family,
M.P.R.W. is an ordinary little boy, delightful in his interactions, polite and
respectful, with a fine curiosity about things, with no observable health problems
and displaying none of the fragilities set out in the mother’s testimony about
him.

(u)    Since his move to the
home of his maternal grandparents almost two years ago, he has had the active
involvement of his maternal grandparents and a maternal aunt in his care.  On
the mother’s uncontradicted evidence, the grandmother collects him from his day
care most days and the aunt takes him to day care in the mornings to free the
mother to attend to her school commitments.  The maternal grandfather has been
a significant, albeit reluctant, transportation assist for the child’s access.

(v)    Despite the comforts of
his life in his grandparents’ home, a number of stresses bear down on M.P.R.W.
as he approaches his 5th birthday.  He risks loss of his day care of the last
eighteen months if no resolution is found for his soiling problem.  He awaits
the clinical examinations and interventions that his mother has lined up for
him.  He still awaits the time when his parents can give him an easy transition
between their respective households.

[
9
]

The mother would have this court find that
M.P.R.W.’s emotional difficulties are tied to Mr. J.W.’s abusive treatment of
both her and the child when they were a family. The evidence as a whole does
not justify such a finding. There is no credible evidence, apart from the single
brief episode of shaking, that this father has ever abused this child either
before or after the parental separation. There is no credible evidence that the
level of conflict between the parents over the course of their time together
rose to a level of “abuse”.  I have dealt with her perceptions on this issue
elsewhere in this judgment.

4.2:     On the Law in the Mother’s Case for Sole Custody

[
10
]

Custody and access claims are governed by
Part III of the
Children’s
Law Reform Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C-12, as amended (the “Act”).

[
11
]

A number of points need to be made in
relation to Ms. A.Z.’s submissions on the law:

(1)    This case is
not

governed by section
29 of the
Act
.  Section
29 of the Act governs
variation
applications — those
applications that seek review of
final
custody orders.  This
child, however, has not yet had a final custody order.  The task of this court
is to provide one for him.

(2)    Proposals once made for
amendment to section
24 of the
Act
(by section 2 of the
Children’s Law Reform Amendment Act,
1989
, S.O. 1989, c. 22, that now languish as section
78 of the current
Children’s
Law Reform Act
under a 15-years layer of dust) have never been and are
not ever likely to be proclaimed in force, nor was the proposed remedy cited by
Ms. A.Z. to deal with access wrongfully denied, including the separation of
wrongful from reasonable denial.

(3)    Ms. A.Z. selected her
case law from the realm of variation, not originating custody.  The case law
advanced in support of her proposition that special deference is owed to her in
this court’s adjudication is case law set in the context of variation where, in
speaking of deference owed to a custodial parent, the court is referencing
parents who have been granted final sole custody orders.

(4)    Ms. A.Z. has no special
claim to this child by operation only of the span of time that she has had
responsibility for the child’s care.  If spans of time alone governed the
outcome, a parent who wanted to thwart a fair consideration of the other
parent’ case could drag the litigation down into a morass of interlocutory
motions and then, as the readiness of the case for a hearing is pushed further
and further into the future, could use the passage of time to claim “victory”.
To try to thwart a fair adjudication of competing claims by strewing the litigation
landscape with interlocutory motions is an abuse of the court’s processes.  It
is also an abuse of the child’s other parent and of the child himself.  Under
the
Children’s
Law Reform Act
, children are entitled to have disputes about their
future care and custody set down for trial within 6 months after the
commencement of the case, and given the earliest possible hearing time.  See section
26 of the Act.  They are not expected to wait eternally for finality to
their parents’ dispute.

[
12
]

The law that she needed to keep in mind is
essentially this:

(a)    Before the parental
separation, she and the father had
equal
entitlement to the custody
of this child.  When they separated and the child continued in her care with
the consent or acquiescence of Mr. J.W., she gained the authority
temporarily

to exercise the rights and responsibilities of custody until a separation
agreement or court order provided otherwise.  See subsection
20(7).  Mr. J.W.’s exercise of his entitlement to custody and the incidents
of custody were
suspended
, not ended.  Such suspension remains in
place only until a separation agreement or court order provides otherwise.  See
subsection
20(4).  The sort of separation agreement meant by this provision is one
that is a valid separation agreement under Part IV of the
Family
Law Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. F-3, as amended.  See subsection
18(1).  There is no such agreement in this case.

(b)    She was given an
ex
parte
order for
temporary
custody of M.P.R.W. when she first
came before the court on 8 January 2001.  At the best of times, temporary orders are temporary solutions
for a child’s ongoing care pending resolution of the court case.  Those orders
are made on partial and untested evidence.  A temporary order made without
proper notice of the motion to the child’s other parent is the most temporary
of temporary orders, resting as it does on evidence not even exposed at that
point to the other parent.

(c)    Ms. Z. has enjoyed her
temporary custody over such a protracted time, not because judges in the course
of judicial case management have decided in her favour on the ultimate outcome
of what is in this child’s best interests, as she argues, but because the
child’s father has supported the child’s remaining in her primary care.

(d)    A custody order is not a
right granted for the benefit of a parent.  It is a legal mechanism through
which a parent discharges responsibilities to the child and it is a heavy
responsibility.  The
Act
requires the person entrusted with custody, whether it
be under the authority of a temporary or a final order, to exercise those
rights and responsibilities, not in the parent’s best interests, but
in
the ongoing best interests of the child
— see subsection
20(2) — and in tune with statutory and court-ordered obligations that are
part and parcel of that custody responsibility.

(e)
Not

suspended, when parents separate and the child remains in the care of one of
them, is the other parent’s entitlement to access to their child — an
entitlement that includes the right to visit with and be visited by the child.
See subsection
20(4) and subsection
20(5).

Ms. A.Z. has had no
right, by virtue of her temporary custody order or in the period prior to any
court order, to deny the child access to his father or to dictate the terms of
that child’s access

(f)
Not

suspended when parents separate and their child remains in the care of one of
them is the entitlement of the other parent to information bearing on the child
— an entitlement identical to that of the parent with actual custody to make
inquiries and be given information as to the health, education and welfare of
the child.  See subsection
20(4) and subsection
20(5).

Ms. A.Z. has had no
right, by virtue of her temporary custody, to withhold information bearing of
the child’s well being from the father.

(g)    A person’s past conduct,

if it is found to be more than allegation
, is not relevant to a
determination of custody or access
unless the conduct is relevant to the
ability of the person to act as a parent to the child
.  See subsection
20(3).

[
13
]

The merits of the competing claims in
relation to this child’s custody are determined from what the trial evidence
yields about what likely lies in M.P.R.W.’s best interests now and for the
foreseeable future — see subsection
24(1) — considering all his needs and circumstances, including those
specifically enumerated in subsection
24(2) and subsection
24(3) of the
Act
.  Although a court tries to be sensitive to the needs and
desires of each parent, it is the child’s needs and interests, as they are
found by the court on the whole of the evidence in the trial, that take
priority.

[
14
]

Final custody adjudications are serious
business.  A final custody order is the outward and visible sign of a court’s
trust in the parent to manage the responsibilities of custody in a manner that
gives priority to the child’s needs and interests.

[
15
]

Although not a determinative factor, a
primary care spanning a period of almost five years receives a very careful
scrutiny in the adjudication of what final custody order is likely to serve the
child’s ongoing and future interests.  In resolving custody disputes, bonding,
attachment and stability are critical considerations for a court.  See for
example,
Barnes
v. Parks
(2001),
2001 CanLII 24146 (ON CA)
, 141 O.A.C. 362, [2001] O.J. No. 643, 2001 Cars­well­Ont
486 Ont. C.A.).

[
16
]

When a temporary custody order has been in
place for such extended time, it is part of the trial court’s evaluation of the
child’s best interests to assess the extent to which the parent entrusted with
the child’s temporary care has carried out his or  her responsibilities to the
child.  It is the quality within the quantity of time under the temporary
custody order that is the focus.

[
17
]

With this backdrop, let me now move to the
findings of fact made in relation to the sole custody claim.

4.3:     On Continuity of Care for M.P.R.W.

[
18
]

I made the following findings:

(a)    Over the course of his
life to date, and not unexpectedly, M.P.R.W. has laid down roots in his
mother’s care, signalling the mother’s ability and motivation to nurture that
rootedness.

(b)    M.P.R.W. had also laid
down roots in the home of his maternal grandparents, who have shown an
impressive generosity and strong commitment to the welfare of both the mother
and this grandson.

(c)    Since August 2002, this
boy has enjoyed a lifestyle in their home that he would not have had in the
care of either his mother or his father, had either been parenting him alone.

(d)    Their generosity has
enabled his mother to complete her education without holding even part-time
employment.  It has given M.P.R.W. a fully funded full-time community based day
care.

(e)    The maternal family has
laid down significant achievement in the management of life.  The
uncontradicted evidence of the mother and maternal grandfather is that the
child’s maternal uncle is a developmental paediatrician, with children of his
own.  M.P.R.W.’s maternal aunt and grandmother are teachers.  His grandfather
is a retired businessman, still engaged in some consulting assignments.  Ms.
A.Z. herself has acquired a university degree over the course of this
litigation and was closing in on certification in paralegal communications.
They are a fortunate family, in fortunate circumstances, and their efforts to
do well are good role modeling for M.P.R.W.

[
19
]

Provided this environment is not used,
directly or indirectly, as a setting within which to alienate the child from
his father, it is in M.P.R.W.’s best interests to preserve the continuity of
his care in his grandparents’ home until the mother, who has not had any long
term full-time employment over the course of M.P.R.W.’s life, is able through
her own employment earnings to lay down a reasonable security for both herself
and M.P.R.W. to augment Mr. J.W.’s financial contribution to M.P.R.W.’s costs.

[
20
]

However, contrary to the mother’s
expectation, a sole custody order in her favour does not emerge from the trial
evidence as the obvious option within which to serve M.P.R.W.’s present and
ongoing best interests.

[
21
]

Let me now move to the findings of fact in
that regard.

4.4:     On the Mother’s Management of her Temporary
Custody Responsibility

[
22
]

On the whole of the trial evidence, this
mother fell significantly short in four areas of her responsibility to this
child:

(1)    her duties
regarding this child’s right of access to his father;

(2)    her
information-sharing responsibility;

(3)    her duty to give
a timely obedience to orders of the court; and

(4)    her duty to keep
her own needs separate from the needs and interests of this child and to defer
own needs in order to meet M.P.R.W.’s needs and interests.

[
23
]

This mother’s irresponsibility in these
areas flows, on the whole of the evidence, from her own neediness.  Over the
course of this protracted litigation, that neediness has threaded itself into
this boy’s life and the life of his father to a degree that is quite worrying.

4.5:     On Her Management of Access and Her Motivation
and Ability to Include the Father in This Child’s Life

[
24
]

The mother’s neediness has been most
prominently manifested in her inadequate management of this child’s access to
his father.  Viewed in isolation, the access history chart prepared by the
mother (exhibit 19) would give the impression that she has regularly and
faithfully made this child available for access.  On the whole of the evidence,
she has actually made it very difficult for this little boy to sustain and grow
his relationship with his father.  Her decision-making in this area has been
mediocre at best and at times frankly irresponsible and mean-spirited.

[
25
]

A child with an access order in place to
govern his contacts with his non-primary care parent should be able to count on
his primary care parent to carry out both the spirit and the letter of the
court’s orders, to keep pace with the variations made to those orders and to
make it as easy as possible for him to grow his relationship with his other
parent.  This child has not had that from his mother.  This child has required
the stimulus of successive orders of the court to keep alive his access at a
community-based access centre, then to expand it to unsupervised access and
ultimately to give him the alternate weekend access that was his routine at the
time of trial.

[
26
]

At times critical to the healthy growth of
his relationship with his father, M.P.R.W. has required a heavy hand of the
court to keep his mother steering in the direction needed to serve his needs
and interests, as the
court
has determined them.  There have been
times, even with the court’s hand at her back, that she has veered outside the
boundaries of the orders made for this child, seemingly unconcerned about her
disobedience and, in that regard, she has had the unfortunate support of the
maternal grandfather.  The result for this child has been a welter of conflict
and hurdles in the implementation of his access from which he could and should
have been spared.  What this mother and maternal grandfather father have not
sufficiently understood is that the court’s temporary access orders are outward
and visible sign that the court, on the evidence flowing before it over the
course of judicial case management, has decided that it is in the child’s best
interests to have
both
parents in his life.  Their feelings to
the contrary do not provide licence to ignore the court’s orders.

[
27
]

For a full 8 months after the parental
separation in December 2000, not­with­standing an access order made on the
second appearance of the case in this court,  M.P.R.W. had no contact with his
father at all.

[
28
]

His mother made no arrangements for contact
either before or after she left the family home on 21 December 2000.  The “no
access, no contact” order that she obtained on her own evidence on 8 January 2001 prohibited all father-and-child contact.
When that prohibition was ended, with her consent, on 30 January 2001 and
replaced with a court order for interim interim supervised access for the child
and the father at a community-based access centre, she failed to carry out her
part of the pre-access intake process.  It took almost six months and an order
of the court ultimately obtained on 15 June 2001 permitting the father to pay
the entire access centre fee with her part of the fee reduced from his child
support payments and a term that she complete the intake requirement within
seven days, to resolve the initial intake problems.

[
29
]

I considered the reasons for her failure to
complete the access centre intake requirements in a timely fashion — namely,
her inability to afford her portion of the access fee, her concern that the
access centre insisted that she sign a release absolving them of all
responsibility in the event of injury to the child while in their care, her
belief that she was not responsible for fulfilling her responsibility for access,
since child support was not yet flowing to her and that meant to her that the
father was not fulfilling his obligations, a notion that had its roots in the
contract “law” she had learned in high school.  None provided an insurmountable
barrier for her, had she been inclined to try to make the access happen for the
child.  It is reasonable to have expected her to borrow the modest fee from her
family, or to bring her problem to the attention of her then counsel with a
view to finding a solution, equally reasonable for her to have informed herself
on the limitations of a waiver of liability and the relevance of high school
contract law to the law governing this litigation.  Her evidence was that she
had been unaware that the terms of the consent had been incorporated into a
court order on 30 January 2001.  Even if I had believed her on that point — and
I did not — she had committed herself in that consent, albeit reluctantly, to
an access plan for this child in return for the father’s ongoing consent to her
temporary custody of M.P.R.W.  It is reasonable to have expected her to honour
the plan.  Instead, she sat back and allowed the gap in contact between the
child and his father to widen.  Her stance left the child with no access at
all.

[
30
]

Her passivity even after resolution of the
access centre’s intake problems resulted in further delay in the start-up of
access for M.P.R.W.  On her evidence, the access centre never contacted her to
set up access until sometime in August 2001. She did not know why.  She made no
inquiries to find out why.  A parent centred on the child’s right to that
access would not have displayed such disinterest in implementation of the
court’s order.

[
31
]

Difficulties in her own ability to transport
the child for his access made the process of exchange a misery for her and by
extension, for the child and his father.  Once access was ready to proceed, the
mother discovered that the route was too difficult for her.

[
32
]

Without a “wheelchair access”, she could not
bring the stroller to the subway station.  On her reasoning, that meant that
she had to carry the child the entire way.  M.P.R.W. was “somewhat resistant”,
making it hard to manage him.  His “supplies” weighed “quite a bit on their
own” and her “back was messed up from a car accident that had happened in
1989”.  These were surmountable obstacles, had she been seriously interested in
giving this child what the court had ordered for him.  Her overload could have
been eased by taking less with her, or having someone from her “support system”
take the child to his access or accompany her in a taxi.

[
33
]

It was not until 25 August 2001 that this child finally had
the contact with his father that the court had ordered on 30 January 2001.  A
responsible parent would have known that, for children so young, frequency of
contact is an important means of keeping the child and parent in tune with each
other and, conversely, that a yawning gap in contact for a child so young would
make it particularly difficult for both him and the father to come together
again.  And sure enough, that happened.  The father was a virtual stranger to
the not-quite-two year-old who came to that first visit.

[
34
]

On her own evidence, the mother “did not get
along very well with the access centre,” in part because she “didn’t feel that
they were providing enough supervision” and her concerns fell on deaf ears.

[
35
]

A hurt shoulder prompted her to suspend the
access altogether on 20 November 2001.  She provided no indication to the father or to the access centre
when she might lift her suspension.  She told this court that she had hurt her
shoulder “from constantly carrying the weight” of items needed for the access,
and had to go to the hospital, instead of delivering the child for access,
because she was “in such excruciating pain”.  She testified that she called the
access centre “as soon as I knew where I stood on it”, told it that she had
been injured and thar she “didn’t know when [she] would be able to bring
M.P.R.W. as a result”.  That decision left the child with no access that day,
and with no plan to resume it.

[
36
]

It took a court order on 19 December 2001,
in response to the father’s motion, to restore the access to this child.  The
mother quite sensibly in the circumstances settled the motion by offering to
make up the visits missed.  The issue is not the legitimacy of the pain that
got in the way of her production of the child for access on 20 November 2001.  She produced medical evidence
that she had received emergency attention that day at Sunnybrook-Women’s College Hospital, and had been sent home
with a diagnosis of tendonitis-bursitis.  The larger issue is why she took no
responsibility for making alternative arrangements to get the child to the
access centre.  Her injury was not the child’s injury.  There were alternatives
for M.P.R.W., had either the mother or the grandfather been inclined to provide
them for M.P.R.W.  I was particularly puzzled by the ease with which the
maternal grandfather fed his daughter’s breach of the court’s order, concluding
that he himself would offer no assistance because, like the mother, he did not
agree with the court’s order.

[
37
]

Now, instead of getting M.P.R.W. to his
access in accordance with the court’s order, the mother offered Mr. J.W. access
with the child in their home under the grandfather’s supervision while she
recovered from her injury.  According to the mother’s evidence, the father
turned down that offer, “claiming that he had paid for the access centre and
wanted to get his money’s worth”.  I am satisfied by the father’s evidence that
this was not the only or even the primary reason that he declined the
proposal.  He wanted to keep in place the routine that he and M.P.R.W. had
developed in the centre, to keep the access in view of those who could attest
to his developing skill with M.P.R.W. in the hope that the mother would grow to
trust his abilities and reduce her resistance and to stay in compliance with
the court’s order.  Those decisions of that father were child-centred and
responsible in the circum­stances.

[
38
]

A variation to the interim access ordered on
consent of the parties on 13 June 2002 and believed by the mother to be the “best representation of
M.P.R.W.’s best interests” created more problems than it resolved.  The
agreement endorsed by the court that day was the end result of discussions
started by the parties during their appearance in the Small Claims Court
earlier that month, furthered by the maternal grandfather, and ultimately
accepted by the father, essentially because it would provide unsupervised
access for him and the child on certain terms.  After waiting patiently for
some 21 months for the mother to become comfortable with his parenting and to
develop his growing relationship with M.P.R.W. within the supervised access
centre, he saw the agreement as a new start in their ability and commitment to
cooperate in M.P.R.W.’s interests.

[
39
]

It soon emerged that he was wrong.  The
father tried to arrange unsupervised access as quickly as possible, wanting to
take advantage of the summer weather.  The mother resisted, telling him that he
“needed to be patient and learn how to take care of M.”  Her reference point
for that was the agreement itself.

[
40
]

Had he read the agreement carefully, he
would have seen that the decision-maker on each successive stage in access
expansion was either the mother or some unnamed third party and that the
agreement was chock full of conditions that made a move forward in the child’s
access virtually impossible.

[
41
]

It purported to give unsupervised access to
the child only after the father had satisfied an array of conditions.  Some
made good sense.  Others were frankly ridiculous.  The father was first to
“child proof” his home, a reasonable enough prerequisite for M.P.R.W., but this
child-proofing had to be “according to legal standards and  . . .
confirmed by an agreed upon third party”.  That left unclear what the legal
standards were and were not, who the third party would be and what particular
expertise would be brought to bear on that decision.  It read like a city
building inspection.  Similarly, the father was to provide, amongst other
items, an appropriate car seat — also a reasonable enough prerequisite if one
was not otherwise available for the child (the father had no car) — but this
car seat had to be “verified by the party responsible for transferring access”.
The meaning of that was wholly unclear.  The inference invited is that it was
either the mother or the maternal grandfather.  The access was to proceed in a
“gradual fashion” — also reasonable enough — but this gradual fashion was
geared to the father’s “obtaining the skills needed to care for M.P.R.W. for
the period of the time of access”.  Who was to assess that?  It was a term that
“in the event of illness” the child was to be returned to mother “immediately
so that she may care for him” — thus sending the message that the father was
wholly incapable of caring for the child himself if illness emerged in a visit.

[
42
]

The mother and grandfather need only put
themselves in the shoes of a person expected to comply with this “agreement” to
appreciate that it was set up to make compliance virtually impossible.  It did
not serve this child’s needs.  It positioned the child for further obstacles in
the growth of his relationship with his father that, in the end, I found to be
its true purpose.

[
43
]

In assessing the father’s casual attention
to the content of the agreement, I took into account that the negotiations took
place at a time when he was still grieving the death of his mother earlier that
spring.  She had been his closest confidant and advisor over the course of his
life.  He admitted that he had not spent a lot of time weighing the pros and
cons of the agreement.  He saw it as a means of gaining the unsupervised access
to M.P.R.W. that he had been working so hard to achieve and did not look
further.

[
44
]

This agreement gave the mother a
micromanagement and “policing” role wholly disproportionate to the need of
either the child or the father for her “supervision”.  That intent to “police”
flowed unchecked again in her proposal of 4 September 2002 (exhibit 37) to the father;
required the father to complete an anger management course, join a parent
support group “immediately” and “provide documentation to confirm that he has
done this”, provide “at least two changes of clothing and footwear that are
size and weather appropriate which are confirmed by receipts prior to the next
access visit that they are needed for” and “an age appropriate bed that is
verified by purchase receipt and photos to show the bed is safely accessible
for naps and for sleeping overnight”.  That proposal also made all increases in
unsupervised access dependent on the father’s continuing “to develop his
parenting skills in accordance paragraph of the June 13, 2002 order and
maintaining the counselling and support network needed to do this”.  These and
other attempts to put in place her own policing of the father’s care were
misguided.  The father had shown himself perfectly capable of managing the
tasks of parenting at that point.

[
45
]

By August 2002 and with the mother and child
now residing in the home of the maternal grandparents in Richmond Hill, M.P.R.W. now had to deal
with a significantly greater transportation time to and from his access to his
father.  The mother considered it too “hard” for her to take him to the access
centre to which he had become accustomed.  She proceeded to make arrangements
with an access centre in York Region.  She invited no input from the father on
that plan.  Eventually, the father agreed to use the York Region centre
(exhibit 8), but not before trying to persuade her to have the restraining
order against him lifted so that they could meet somewhere not so far removed
from Toronto for the access exchange.  She refused because she did not want an
association with the father.  It was not until October 2002 that M.P.R.W. was
produced for access at the centre in York Region.  It was a mystery to her why
the father had resisted her plan.  It was a mystery to this court why she had
not considered how much easier she could have made the exchange for both
M.P.R.W. and his father at that stage in the development of the father-and-son
relationship, and why, unless intent on making things particularly onerous on
the father, she was asking him to travel such a long distance by public transit
both in Toronto and in York Region to collect the child.

[
46
]

It took a further court order to give the
child and father an easier means of coming together for their access.  On 16
October 2002, the case management judge set aside the order made 13 June 2002
in the context of a motion brought by the mother to terminate the father’s
access for his breaches of the June agreement, removed the supervised access
exchange component from the child’s life altogether and expanded the child’s
access, on specified terms, to alternate weekend overnight access, with M.P.R.W.
to be exchanged at a specific midtown subway station at a specific time on
Saturday mornings and Sunday afternoons.  The child was also given compensatory
access for the visits missed and an expanded Christmas access with his father.

[
47
]

The mother responded with a motion to set
aside that order and a failure to produce the child for his visits on 26
October and on 9 November 2002.
Her motion was unsuccessful.  On 3 December 2002, Justice Lynn King of this
court ordered the access to go forward as stipulated in the order of 16 October 2002, with an additional condition
imposed on the agreement of the parents that M.P.R.W. not be left alone with
his paternal grandfather during access.  On 3 February 2003, Justice King
expanded the child’s alternate weekend access further from Fridays at 5:30 p.m. to Sundays at 7:00 p.m.  The mother’s
appeals of these orders were ultimately dismissed on 12 May 2003 by Justice Peter G. Jarvis of the
Ontario Superior Court.

[
48
]

Although the mother had laid down a measure
of better co-operation as the case approached trial, her attempt to undo
provisions made for the child by the court resurfaced in the course of the
trial.  With additional days still needed to complete the trial, the parents
were directed by the court to make better transportation arrangements for this
boy to reduce his travel time by public transit.  The parents’ negotiations
resulted in a consent order of 17 March 2004 that the mother would take
responsibility for bringing the child to his access.  She then tried to
withdraw that consent when the trial resumed.  I declined her desire to change
the arrangements.  Her concerns about the disruption to the family dinner, the
lateness of the child’s bedtime in his father’s home, the travel time and her
desire to reduce the sleepovers to only one night on the alternate weekends
have all been considered by this court in the context of the evidence as a
whole bearing on this boy’s best interests.

[
49
]

The mother would have this court find that
the child has no meaningful relationship with his father and that their contact
with each other is not something worth sustaining for M.P.R.W.  There is no
credible evidence to support either finding.  M.P.R.W. has yet to receive from
his mother a solid endorsement that his father has a value and importance in
his life, essentially because his mother is so certain that her own poisonous
view of the father is the only valid view.

[
50
]

The reports prepared by the community-based
access centre over the course of its supervision of the father-child access
between 25 August 2001 and 24 August 2002 (exhibit 17) are glowing testament of
this child’s growing joy in his time with his father and of the father’s
ability and motivation to keep himself centred on the needs of the child during
access and at times of transition.  The observations of father and child
undertaken by the investigator at the Office of the Children’s Lawyer were
similar.  M.P.R.W.’s maternal grandmother testified to the child’s excitement
about visits with his father.  The father’s friends, who have joined in
M.P.R.W.’s weekend access with their own children, testified to the easy
interaction between the child and his father, the nature of the father’s
parenting while they have been present, the child’s respect for his father and
their general enjoyment of each other.  In their eyes, M.P.R.W. is “an ordinary
little kid” enjoying time with “his Daddy”.  Their observations are consistent
with what has been observed by the extended paternal family who testified in
the trial.

[
51
]

It is irresponsible for this mother to blind
herself to the perceptions of others about this child’s experience of his
father.  Her beliefs about this father and child need re-examination and a
parent centred on the child’s needs would long ago have undertaken that task.

[
52
]

I found one particular failure of the mother
and maternal grandfather to produce the child for his access especially
troubling, essentially because it laid bare an alliance between this mother and
maternal grandfather that had been percolating through the trial and causing
increasing concern to the court because its goal appeared to be to defeat this
child’s right of access to his father.

[
53
]

Aunt H.W. had come to Toronto to share in the father’s
celebration of the child’s birthday.  When Aunt H.W. drove to the home of the
maternal grandparents in a good-faith effort to provide the transportation to
the father’s home for the scheduled visit, with father in tow, with the child
car seat, and in anticipation of collecting M.P.R.W., the grandfather’s
response was that it was “not feasible” to allow the child to go with them.  No
reason was given to her — even when she tried to explain that she had driven to
Toronto from Belleville to celebrate the child’s
birthday with him.  He wanted to know whether she was available to drive the
child back and provide transportation on an ongoing basis.  She was not.  She
works most weekends.  The child was never produced.  He was seen by his Aunt
H.W. playing in the front window with the blinds.  The attitudes and actions of
both the grandfather and the mother made no common sense, on the whole of the
evidence bearing on that proposed visit.  The grandfather busied himself with
taking down the licence number of the vehicle.  The mother’s response to Aunt
H.W.’s arrival was to call the police because she felt “threatened”.  I
searched long and hard for “threat” within the interaction that day and found
none.  I found instead an astonishing display of callous disregard for a little
boy’s opportunity for a birthday celebration with an aunt who had come a
considerable distance to visit him — a celebration that was denied him by both
his mother and his grandfather.

[
54
]

For all the foregoing reasons, this court
had real concern about this mother’s  motivation to respect and nurture this
child’s right to have his father a consistent and valued presence in his life,
or to obey orders of the court designed to respect that right.

4.6:     On the Mother’s Motivation and Ability to Give
Obedience to Orders of the Court

[
55
]

It is not just in relation to access that
Ms. A.Z. has tried to deflect and ultimately to defeat orders made by the
court.  In relation to the order of the case management judge requiring an
investigation and report to the court by the Office of the Children’s Lawyer to
shed independent light on the circumstances of the child and his parents, she
succeeded in undermining the intent of the order altogether.

[
56
]

Her mistrust of the investigation
effectively deprived the child of the benefits intended by the court’s order.
Custody was not in issue at that point.  The investigation was intended to
explore what sort of access made sense for this child, taking into account the
circumstances of parent, and whether the concerns of either emerged as concerns
for the Office of the Children’s Lawyer.  The social worker, Ms. Chodos, was
unable to gain the cooperation of the mother in the investigation.

[
57
]

The mother showed no real commitment to
getting the child to his father’s home for the observational visit that the
social worker needed at the time to inform her investigation.  Whether the
originally scheduled visit was missed because of mis­communication or
otherwise, the social worker and the father, who had taken time off work to
accommodate the observational visit, sat waiting for a child who never did arrive.
On her own evidence, Ms. A.Z. ultimately told Ms. Chodos that she would ask her
father to drive the child, but then “M.P.R.W. got sick and I had to take him to
the doctor’s and there was no meeting confirmed, so it got forgotten”.

[
58
]

When the social worker sought her consent to
speak with certain persons likely to have information to assist in a fair
investigation, the mother considered her to be “ making attacks on my
character”.  Supported by the maternal grandfather, the mother then set about
to attack the competence and professionalism of the social worker, accusing her
of bias against her.

[
59
]

Ms. Chodos was questioned at length in the
trial by the mother, father’s counsel and the court.  I found no incompetence.
Nor did I find bias.  I found a social worker, initially puzzled and then
increasingly exasperated by the mother’s attitude and conduct, who on her own
investigation, did not share the mother’s opinions about the father and his
parenting and who would have liked to have had the co-operation of the mother
in the investigation.

[
60
]

It was not that the mother did not
understand what was required of her in that investigation.  On her own
evidence, the mother, then represented by counsel, understood it to be her responsibility
under that order to “comply with what they wanted”.  Her resistance grew as the
Office of the Children’s Lawyer, relying on the positive information provided
to her by the supervised access centre and the good working relationship that
she had from the child’s father, began to explore an expansion of the access
for the child.  In her mind the social worker was favouring the respondent,
“doing everything possible to assist [him]”.

[
61
]

What emerges from the evidence bearing on
that investigation — the bulk of it from the mother and the documents filed by
her in relation to it — is not that she could not see, but that she
would

not see why the social worker was recommending a lessening of the restrictions
on this child’s access with his father.  Essentially, this mother could not
abide information from the Office of the Children’s Lawyer that was
inconsistent with her own beliefs about the value of his father to this child.

[
62
]

On the whole of the evidence bearing on that
investigation — most of it her own, including the array of correspondence that
moved between her and the Office of the Children’s Lawyer, and between her
father and the Office of the Children’s Lawyer — she made no solid attempt,
consistent with the temporary custody responsibility entrusted to her by the
court, to work with the social worker to accomplish a fair and full
investigation that had been ordered by the court.  I looked for some
recognition either from her or from her father that the court order had been
wholly undermined by their actions and attitude toward the investigator and the
investigation itself.  I found none. The need to malign the social worker
overwhelmed any meaningful concern for their duty to respect the order that had
requisitioned that investigation.

4.7:     On the Mother’s Management of Her Information Sharing
Responsibility

[
63
]

Over the course of this litigation, this
mother has shown no particular interest in keeping the father in the
information “loop” on matters affecting the wellbeing of their son.  It was her
evidence that the father has never asked.  On the whole of the evidence, I find
that he could certainly have been asking more often, but I am satisfied that he
did attempt to gain information and was deflected.  His outreach to the child’s
physician earlier in the case produced no information but rather a response
that suggested a real animosity towards him.  The court had given him
opportunity to get to know the child’s day-care providers when he collected
M.P.R.W. for access.  That was scuttled when the child was removed from that
day care.  It was evident in the trial that this father had had no meaningful
information about the interventions that awaited M.P.R.W. at the close of the
trial.  Not even the identity of certain of the clinicians was made known to
him, or indeed to the court, until the trial was stood down so that the mother
could obtain the information by telephone.

[
64
]

I did not conclude, on the whole of the
evidence, that Mr. J.W. was disinterested in the M.P.R.W.’s well being, as the
mother had argued.  He did choose not to battle with Ms. A.Z. for information
about M.P.R.W.  It was not unreasonable, with so much else in dispute, to
proceed on the basis that, as she learned to share M.P.R.W., she would learn to
share information about M.P.R.W.  The result for the boy was nonetheless a father
who had no input into the various medical and other interventions arranged for
him by his mother, no information flowing to the father about the need for
those interventions, no opportunity for him to be supported through those
interventions by his father and a father flying blind on what, if anything,
apart from what the mother was demanding of him, the child needed from him
during their times of access in relation to those interventions; whether it be
special care, special foods, special provisions.

[
65
]

I am satisfied by the evidence that the
father did ask for information about the well being of this boy and was
deflected to the point where he chose not to press the issue.  It did not
signal that he was not worried about the child.

[
66
]

A reasonable parent, centred on the child’s
well being, does not exclude the other parent from information bearing on the
child’s well being.  To do that suggests that there is something secretive
about the information.  Concern about secrecy and what may be underlying the secrecy
festers over time.  This child needs and is entitled to have openness between
his parents on all matters bearing on his well being.

4.8:     On the Mother’s Motivation to Keep the Child’s
Needs and Interests Separate from Her Own Needs

[
67
]

On the whole of the trial record, I find
that this mother has a strong and abiding need to have  her own needs met first
and at times exclusively.  That need has played itself out in the mother’s
tendency to magnify things so far out of proportion to reality that she blinds
herself to a reasoned perspective on both her own conduct, the conduct of
others and the impact of either on M.P.R.W.

[
68
]

It began with the manner in which she
pursued this litigation.  Whatever Ms. A.Z. placed before the motions judge on 8 January 2001 in support of her claims for
emergency relief, including her claim for a no-access, no-contact order, it was
clear that, on the
trial
evidence bearing on that time, there was
no need for emergency relief that day or at any other time.  Her action
appeared to have been a deliberate attempt to exclude the father from any
participation in that initial court appearance in an attempt to gain an
advantage over him — a strategy wholly unnecessary, since there was no threat
at all to her continued custody of the child at that time.  She had, in fact,
disrupted a planned separation.  M.P.R.W. never did get the benefit of that
planning.  She left the family home with the child on 21 December 2000, after
the father had gone to work.

[
69
]

There was no credible evidence in the trial
to support her “sense” that Mr. J.W. had given her a “threatening” look the
previous evening and that she had had to “run for her life” the next day.  The
father came home from work on 21 December 2000 to find her and the child gone.  On the next day, he received a
telephone call from her demanding that he vacate the apartment by 31 December
2000, failing which she would call the police to have him removed.
That

was the sort of threat that unleashed havoc for both of them a mere three days
before Christmas — the upheaval for both herself and the child as she decided
where and how long to stay outside the family apartment, no reasonable
opportunity for the father, working a fulltime job and equally responsible for
the lease on the family home, to obtain alternative affordable accommodations
and furnishings within the time limit set by her, a spoiled Christmas for the
father, no opportunity for the child to have contact with his father.  A parent
better in control of her impulsivity would not have behaved in such a
capricious fashion.

[
70
]

In some ways, this mother has shown a good
ability to recognize and respond to M.P.R.W.’s needs.  Her response in the
immediate aftermath of the shaking incident was thoroughly responsible.  The
shaking of a vulnerable infant is something to be taken very seriously.  She
sought prompt medical assessment of the infant, undertook proper follow up with
medical staff at the Hospital for Sick Children to make sure that she was both
fully informed on what the infant needed from her and that she acted on the
instructions given to her.  She also acted in a responsible fashion when she
found that she could not manage the child’s out-of-control behaviour and sought
help for both herself and the boy from the Hincks-Dellcrest Centre.

[
71
]

In other ways, the mother’s conduct raises
real question that she has allowed her anxiety about this boy’s welfare to
float unconnected to his realities.  For example, on the whole of the trial
evidence, it is not at all clear whether this mother has heard the results of
the clinical assessment of
this particular shaking
.  This child
was not injured by it.  The cautions in the medical report of Dr. Shouldice, if
read carefully and in context, warn against repercussions for the child if
he
were to be subjected to any future shaking
.  There has been no further
shaking.

[
72
]

There is a disconcerting undercurrent in the
various interventions that the mother has arranged for the child.  She sees
fragility in this child where no other witness has seen fragility.  Absent
evidence from these various clinicians — and there was none in the trial — the
question is whether these interventions are undertaken, not because M.P.R.W.’s
needs call out for them, but because the mother needs to fan her own beliefs
about his fragility.

[
73
]

A parent’s perceptions affect that person’s
parenting.  As a matter of common sense, distorted perceptions can wreak havoc
on a child.  A child perceived erroneously as “fragile” may be undeservedly
sheltered from the “rough and tumble” that is an ordinary part of childhood,
might not be taught inner controls with the same vigour that one would use with
a “stronger’ child, might not be allowed to grow to his potential because
expectations of him are too low.

[
74
]

In other areas of her judgment, the mother
insists on a single explanation for a problem that she has identified in
M.P.R.W. when it is obvious that there are other explanations, equally worthy
of consideration, for this child’s reactions to stress.

[
75
]

This mother has tied this child’s
difficulties to the aftermath of the parental separation to the conduct of his
father.  For reasons set out elsewhere in this judgment, I found no conduct in
the father that would reasonably make him the sole or even contributing cause
of the child’s difficulties.

[
76
]

The mother is convinced that the child’s
difficult behaviour after access to his father is “trauma” from the exposure to
the father — whether it be his willingness to go shopping with her and his
grandfather after an access visit, or his resistance to having his coat taken off
when he arrives at his grandparents’ home, or his readiness to test her mettle
by floating comments about his experience that accord with what he believes she
would like to hear.

[
77
]

There is no credible evidence in the trial
that this boy’s exposure to his father is traumatic to him.  If he is
experiencing “trauma”, it is more likely connected to his increasing sense,
consistent with his growing development, that his mother and grandfather do not
much like this “Daddy” in his life and that he cannot figure out what to do
about that.  Lurking beneath the evidence bearing on this child’s inability to
heed his mother’s directions is a sense that this little boy, so pampered by
his mother, is gaining an unhealthy omnipotence over her.

[
78
]

The child’s experience of access reveals a
mother who has a good understanding on things consistent with her own beliefs,
but who defaults to a lack of understanding when something is asked or expected
of her that she does not wish to hear or to do.  Her coping mechanism at those
times is to stand by, purporting to be “helpless” to figure out what is needed
of her, or alternatively to set about to scuttle the plans and goals of others
equally interested in this boy’s welfare.

[
79
]

Ms. A.Z. has shown no meaningful ability to
connect the child’s difficulties with her own behaviour.  As a matter of simple
human experience, young children are sensitive to the emotions of those who are
responsible for their care and distressed if they experience a distressed
parent.  It is part of the dependency of childhood.  A responsible parent recognizes
that.

[
80
]

It is not that she was blind to her own
fragility.  She gave as illustration an incident where she had had to venture
out on her own with M.P.R.W. in his stroller to take him to the Sick Children’s
Hospital, about a 15-minute walk from their home, and “feeling so scared just
walking down there  . . .  so defenceless”, truly believing that she
could not do things without [the child’s father].

[
81
]

There is an unhealthy selfishness in Ms.
A.Z.’s approach to this child.  To her, M.P.R.W. was and is “my” child, a
distortion that repeatedly seeped through her evidence and persisted, even when
it was drawn to her attention that M.P.R.W. is a child of both his parents.  It
gave credibility to the father’s testimony that, during their time together as
a family, he had difficulty gaining her co-operation in allowing him to develop
his own relationship with their infant son.

[
82
]

It explained much of her resistance to the
child’s access to his father and also her resistance to court orders that paved
the way for the development of the father-and-son relationship.  She can mouth
the words of individualization, and at times quite eloquently.  She is quick to
criticize the father for not equipping himself, as she has done, with formal
parenting courses to meet their son’s ever evolving development.  The
difficulty is that she has yet to be put her words into action consistently and
cohesively for this boy.

[
83
]

Essentially, she wants this child to remain
untouched by any person who does not agree with her perception of his needs and
interests.  Indeed, it was a term of one of the interim agreements in this case
that the father not do anything to “alter” the child.  It is an approach to
parenting that, if left unchecked and undiluted, sends a message to the child
that no one but his mother is a capable caregiver.  That sort of message robs
the child of his ability to lay down trust in others and is ultimately
smothering and destructive.

[
84
]

She had this problem drawn to her attention
over two years ago.  On her own evidence, her counselor at the Hincks Centre
had been concerned that this mother did not seem to “have her own life, that
[her] life revolved around my son a lot”.  When she was asked whether she had
been concerned about that, her reply was that she had not really thought about
it.  To her credit, she did try to do more things for herself; for example,
putting M.P.R.W. in day care for an extra day.  She could say herself that she
“didn’t seem to have much of an identity past my son at that point”.  She still
has a long way to go in that regard.

[
85
]

A measure of upheaval is to be expected in
any family breakdown.  It is taking her longer to rest her agitation about that
breakdown.  She has yet to accept any responsibility for her own role in that
breakdown and has chosen to demonize Mr. J.W.  That, in turn, has caused her
dedication to their child to drift into neuroticism.  If she is to be a
responsible parent, she cannot continue to blind herself to the impact of her
attitudes on this child — specifically, the insecurities that she plants in
him, whether she intends it or not, and the confusions and unnecessary
challenges that she throws in his way.  It is time to accept with equanimity
that life does not always work out as planned, that both parties in a
relationship own responsibility for its health or destruction and that each
party can emerge from it with greater insight and strength.  It is the beauty
of life that, over time, upheaval subsides.  Life does move on.  It requires
work to have it move on well.  The time is long overdue for Ms. A.Z. to put
aside her image of herself as a victim.

[
86
]

Her duty to protect the child from harm
embraces her responsibility to shield the child from excesses in her own
behaviour and beliefs that are likely to cause harm to the child in her care.
She has the ability.  What has been lacking is motivation to see both herself
and the child in a healthier light.

4.9:     On This Mother’s Ability to Manage Her Own Life

[
87
]

But for the problems found in relation to
the management of her parenting, this mother has laid down some impressive
accomplishments in her own life.  She has acquired a university education, the
bulk of it over very difficult years in her life and the life of this child and
his father.  She has a zest for the things legal and, at the close of the
