community college.  She is optimistic about her career potential and, at the
close of trial, had employment opportunities lined up for exploration.  She has
undertaken her own personal development while trying to attend to the needs of
a young child.  She has had a significant measure of support, to be sure, from
her family and community based resources, but that does not detract from the
stamina that she brought to the task.

[
88
]

She is also a woman who, whatever her fears
and lack of confidence in the aftermath of the parental separation, showed
herself capable of take care of both herself and M.P.R.W. in difficult
circumstances.  Finances were tight and her debt load significant.  Her attempt
in 2001 to work for a shoe store ended after two months “because of problems
with subsidy and having to come to court quite often”.  She quite sensibly
reduced her emotional stress somewhat by her decision to graduate with a
general university degree in June 2002 rather than continue to the four-year
degree that had been her aspiration.

[
89
]

Her move to the home of her parents was also
a sensible decision for both herself and the child.  Her graduation from university
marked the end of her entitlement to student housing, subsidized day care and
personal counselling services provided as part of university life.

[
90
]

Her efforts to prepare herself for the
workforce through paralegal training in also sensible.  If this child is to
have the material benefits in life that she wishes for him,
both

parents need to be gainfully employed and both need to wean themselves from
their reliance on the maternal grandparents to give the child that.

[
91
]

This ability to take hold of challenges and
master them can be brought to bear on those attitudes in her parenting that
need a more mature perspective, if she chooses to do that work.

4.10:   On the Applicant Mother’s Case for Supervised
Access or Supervised Access Exchange

4.10(a):   Access between Child
and Father

[
92
]

At the close of the applicant mother’s case
on 15 March 2004, I had
indicated to the parties that there was no need to put the father to the task
of responding to this claim or to the claim for a restraining order against
him.  The mother had not made out an evidentiary case for either order and, in
light of the duty of both parties and the court to manage the litigation in
both a fair and cost-effective manner, it made no common sense to put the
father to the task of responding to claims that never rose above the level of
allegation.  I also took into account that the mother had sought the court’s
assurance that morning, with her case still not completed, that the trial would
finish “this week” because she had a job offer and could not take it until she
was freed from the responsibilities of the trial.

[
93
]

There is nothing in the trial evidence that
warrants the involvement of a supervised access centre in the life of this
child or his father.

[
94
]

Supervised access is a stepping stone to a more
normalized access for a child and parent, reserved for children who require
that sort of support until they and the access parent are able to move forward
in their relationship without that support.  Supervised access also sends
message to the child that either he or the parent need that support — that the
support and supervision are key to his safety or well being in that parent’s
care.  It is a confusing and ultimately pernicious message when it is not
consistent with the realities of the child and parent subjected to the
supervision.

[
95
]

The evidence as a whole does not support a
finding that the father presents any sort of risk to this child, now or for the
foreseeable future, or indeed to Ms. A.Z.

[
96
]

Supervised access also has the effect of
reducing the time for access.  Arrangements must be co-ordinated with the
availability and hours of operation of a centre.  At the time of trial, the
child’s access spanned Friday evenings to Sunday evenings.  In this case,
M.P.R.W. would forego his Friday sleepovers in his father’s home, have
shortened his time with his father on Sundays and make the arrangements for
most holiday access almost impossible.  It is not in this child’s best
interests to diminish his time with his father.

[
97
]

Involvement of a supervised access centre
also costs money.  To use the services of a community-based access centre to
move this child between his two parents would be a misuse of resources and a
waste of money.

[
98
]

This child has not been subjected to a
supervised access for some two years.  The use of a supervised access centre
for the exchange of the child ended in October 2002 by order of the court.
There is nothing in the trial evidence that justifies a “stepping back” of this
child in time.

[
99
]

As an intelligent and responsible parent
cast with the duty of putting the child’s needs and interests ahead of her own
and fairly considering the successful progression of this child beyond the need
for unsupervised access or exchange, Ms. A.Z. ought reasonably to have
recognized that and discontinued these particular claims.

[
100
]

The only risk to this child during any
exchange lies within his mother and the choices that she makes at the time of
each exchange.  As a responsible parent, she is expected to send this child off
into his time with his father without injecting into that transition conduct or
attitude that makes him feel guilty about leaving her.  As a responsible
parent, she is expected to pass on to the father any health care information
reasonably needed by the child during his time with his father (for example, a
need for medication) and otherwise to trust the father to manage the child’s
care responsibly and in the child’s best interests, as is, in fact, his duty
throughout the time that the child is with him.  She is expected to refrain
from injecting her own parenting “rules” and practices into the father’s care,
accepting that there are ways to parent other than her own that are perfectly
fine for a child.  In that fashion, this child learns that he can trust both of
his parents to care for him and that it is fine to love and enjoy the company
of both of his parents.  The mother, if motivated, has the ability to adapt her
conduct and attitudes to accomplish this for M.P.R.W.

4.10(b):  Access between Child and Paternal Grandfather

[
101
]

At the time of trial, it was a condition of
the interim access order that the father not permit the child an unsupervised
access to his paternal grandfather.  The term had been injected into the
court’s order for this child’s access on 3 December 2002, on agreement of the
parents.  Ms. A.Z. seeks have that condition incorporated into any final
order.  In that stance, she is supported by the Office of the Children’s
Lawyer.  Mr. J.W. seeks to have it ended.

[
102
]

The concern bearing on this child’s best
interests is that this grandfather was prosecuted some 10 years ago for the
offence of sexual touching of his then eleven-year-old daughter.  He admitted
his guilt, was thus found guilty and was held accountable for that offence by a
suspended sentence and a term of probation.  The uncontradicted evidence before
me is that he completed his probation.  He had had no criminal record prior to
that offence and has had none since.

[
103
]

Mr. Bhathal has accurately characterized the
evidence provided by Ms. Chodos on the “risk” element advanced as reason for a
restriction on the grandfather’s contact.  It is essentially a stance rooted,
not in anything specific to this child and this grandfather, but in a
proposition that “once labelled, forever labelled”, emerging from some
unidentified teaching given to her.  It is speculation and conjecture, not
evidence of likely risk to the child.

[
104
]

The child pays too high a price for the
restriction sought on his contact with his paternal grandfather.  M.P.R.W.
needs to be able to look to his paternal grandfather from time to time to
assist in transportation where extended family join the father’s parenting
time.  Absent likelihood of risk to the boy in his grandfather’s unsupervised
presence — and I found none — there is no reason to inject conditions into that
contact that makes it harder for this paternal grandfather to do more for his
grandson than he has been free to do until now.

4.11:   On the Applicant’s Mother’s Case for a Restraining
Order against the Father

[
105
]

Orders restraining harassment are governed
by section
35 of the
Act
.

[
106
]

Restraining orders are serious business.
They are reserved for situations where the evidence satisfies the court that a
parent or child in that parent’s care needs protection from the person named in
the order.  These orders are deposited with police services for the purpose of
enforcement.  Breach of the order invites arrest without warrant and
prosecution in the provincial offences court, with liability, on conviction, to
either or both a fine of $5,000 and imprisonment for a term of up to three
months for a first offence and up to 2 years for a subsequent offence.  See subsection
35(2).

[
107
]

As a matter of common sense, restraining
orders make complex all manner of things that need to be kept simple for a
child — arrangements for his contacts with his non-custodial parent, the
ability to involve both of them in his school and community activities to which
parents are ordinarily invited and his image of each parent.  They send a
message to a child that he cannot count on his parents to conduct themselves
courteously in
his
best interests and that their needs and
desires are more important than his own.

[
108
]

A person seeking a restraining order must be
scrupulously fair about the evidence placed before the court for such an
order.  A fear of abusive or threatening conduct must be
reasonably
grounded
.  Allegations that a child’s parent presents a risk, if not
restrained by court order, are not to be flung about for the purpose of
creating mischief for either the child or a non-custodial parent.

[
109
]

Ms. A.Z. would have this court find that Mr.
J.W. abused her during their relationship and that her experience has left her
so scarred that she still lives in fear of a recurrence.  At its highest, this
“fear” is a figment of her imagination.  At its lowest, it is a deliberate
concoction put forth in a misguided attempt both to disown aspects of her own
conduct and attitude that contributed the breakdown of the relationship with
Mr. J.W. and to portray Mr. J.W. as an unfit parent.  An allegation of abuse is
not proof of abuse.  An assertion of fear is not by itself proof that there is
good reason for the fear.

[
110
]

What the evidence yields is this:

(a)    They became disenchanted
with each other over the course of her difficult pregnancy and in the months
following the child’s birth.

(b)    Mr. J.W., rightly or
wrongly — and in the overall scheme of things it is unimportant at this stage
in the life of each of them:

(i)    felt
increasingly excluded from opportunity to nurture his own relationship with the
child

(ii)    felt that he
was increasingly expected to be both errand boy and housekeeper for the mother,

(iii)    was more
concerned about their ability to satisfy their growing debts than she was concerned,
and

(iv)    felt that his
family and friends were not welcome in their home

(c)    She felt, rightly or
wrongly— and at this stage in the overall scheme of things, it is also unimportant
at this stage in their life — that he was not doing enough to support her in
her newly arrived motherhood.

(d)    There were times that
Mr. J.W., tired from his work and less able to bind his frustration and exasperation,
exhibited short temper with her.  Mr. J.W. acknowledged that he had spoken
angry words from time to time.

(e)    Nothing in the evidence
supported a finding that their arguments were anything more than the wear and
tear experienced by two different personalities trying to assert their
differing opinions on things.

(f)    It was Ms. A.Z.’s
hypersensitivity to those expressions of frustration with her conduct that sent
her perceptions into the stratosphere, not anything inherent in Mr. J.W.’s
words or actions.

(g)    Her sudden leaving of
the family home on 21 December 2000 was such an unfolding.  It had nothing to do with any abusive
conduct by Mr. J.W.  It emanated from her perceptions that I have found
elsewhere in these judgment reasons to be a distortion of reality.  She manufactured
her fear and then acted on it.

(h)    Her attention to his
e-mail transmissions are also typical of that hypersensitivity.  Contrary to
her assertion, none of the e-mails from him that were filed in evidence in this
trial provided a basis for finding his tone or language “threatening”.  They
exhibit a real desire to work with her for M.P.R.W.’s interests.  They also
make clear the sincerity of his interest in M.P.R.W. and his preparedness to
work within whatever the court decides is in M.P.R.W.’s best interests in terms
of their father-son relationship.  There is nothing untoward in that.

(i)    The initial “interim
interim” order for “no contact” made without prejudice that she had obtained
without notice to Mr. J.W. on 8 January 2001 was ended on 30 January 2001.  The more general interim
restraining order made with Mr. J.W.’s consent on 30 January 2001 was also
ended a long time ago.

(j)    On the mother’s own
evidence, Mr. J.W. complied with the temporary restraining orders.  She was
unable to point a single instance of conduct since the termination of those
orders that would give rise to a need to restrain his communication or contact
with her.

(k)    Mr. J.W. has no history
of harassment or abuse of a partner, nor does he have a criminal record.

[
111
]

I did not find, when he has sought the
court’s assistance over the course of judicial case management, to reactivate
access that the mother had halted, that he was acting to harass her or to make
her life miserable.  He sought that assistance because he understood the price
that would be paid by the child by those gaps — that if the gap widened too
far, both he and the child would lose ground in the relationship that he was
trying so hard to sustain for both of them.

[
112
]

The evidence as a whole yielded a real
disconnection between Ms. A.Z.’s words of fear and her actions.  She has
actually shown herself quite competent and adept in interactions with Mr. J.W.
over the course of this litigation, when she has perceived a benefit in that
interaction.

[
113
]

I scrutinized with particular care the
evidence of the maternal grandfather on his daughter’s fear — specifically,
that had fed his own belief that Mr. J.W. posed a risk to Ms. A.Z. or the
child.  In the end, but for a telephone call with his daughter in January 2001,
in which he heard Mr. J.W. “yelling” through the apartment door, an incident
credibly explained by Mr. J.W. in his evidence, his perception is rooted in the
accounts told to him by his daughter.  He believed her.  On the whole of the evidence,
I did not.

[
114
]

There is no credible evidence that Mr. J.W.
conducted himself in his interactions with Ms. A.Z. in a manner that was
physically or emotionally abusive to her, that he harassed her or that he
conducted himself in any other manner that would cause fear to a person
reasonably interpreting his words and actions.  But for the shaking incident in
M.P.R.W.’s infancy, there is no credible evidence that he has ever mistreated
his son.

[
115
]

What is apparent from the totality of the
trial evidence is that “fear” is marketed by Ms. A.Z. as a reason for avoiding
something that she does not want to do.  This child’s best interests are not
served by a restraining order imposed only to appease his mother’s
sensibilities.  A parent centred on the needs and interests of this child would
have long ago seen the disconnect between her fear and the father’s conduct and
refused to wallow in a fear so flimsy.  Fears that are irrational are fears to
be overcome.

[
116
]

M.P.R.W. needs his mother to overcome her
fears.

[
117
]

This claim, too, reflects Ms. A.Z.’s attempt
to step back in time.  On the whole of the trial evidence, there never has been
a need for a restraining order against this father.  This particular claim
should have been discontinued long ago.

4.12:   On the Father’s Case for a Joint Custody Order

[
118
]

This is not a case where the father seeks a
joint custody in order to disrupt the child’s primary care with his mother.  He
acknowledges both the rootedness that M.P.R.W. has in his mother’s home and the
supports that the grandparents have provided to M.P.R.W. and wants to preserve
that continuity for M.P.R.W.  Quite apart from his interest in spending more
time with M.P.R.W., to the extent that his work life allows that, he proposes
joint custody as the option needed by M.P.R.W. to deal responsibly with the
following:

(1)    His concern that this
child, appearing quite normal in his growth and development to him, is
requiring such an array of clinical interventions.

(2)    His concern, given his
financial straits, that the mother not incur debt on this child’s behalf in
which he is expected to share proportionately without any input from him.

(3)    His concern about
M.P.R.W.’s ability to manage French immersion schooling, as the mother desires
for him, if he is delayed in aspects of his development, including an apparent
need for speech assessment.

(4)    His concern about the
impact on M.P.R.W. and on him if the mother continues to devalue the father-son
relationship and M.P.R.W.’s exposure to his father is insufficient to sustain
and build the boy’s trust in his father’s parenting.

[
119
]

This latter concern weighs particularly
heavily with him.  He seeks an order of joint custody essentially as a legal
assurance that the child will have his father as a meaningful part of his
life.  He does not trust the mother’s motivation to give M.P.R.W. that.

[
120
]

The mother argues that the absence of
co-operation between her and the father rules out joint custody as a viable
option for M.P.R.W. and that she is supported in that stance by the case law.

[
121
]

The Ontario Court of Appeal has expressed
reservation about the viability of joint custody for a child in high conflict
cases, pointing out that joint decision-making requires the demonstration of a
high degree of co-operation between the parents.  See
Johnson
v. Cleroux
(2002),
2002 CanLII 44929 (ON CA)
, 159 O.A.C. 346, 24 R.F.L. (5th) 422, [2002] O.J. No.
1801, 2002 Cars­well­Ont 1559 (Ont. C.A);
Hildinger
v. Carroll
(2004),
2004 CanLII 13456 (ON CA)
, 128 A.C.W.S. (3d) 1143, [2004] W.D.F.L. 167, [2004]
O.J. No. 291, 2004 Cars­well­Ont 444 (Ont. C.A.), affirming

(2002), 112 A.C.W.S. (3d) 84,  [2002] O.J. No. 572
, 2002 Cars­well­Ont 526
(Ont. S.C.), affirming the continuing relevance of
Baker v. Baker

(1979),
1979 CanLII 1962 (ON CA)
, 23 O.R. (2d) 391, 95 D.L.R. (3d) 529, 8 R.F.L. (2d) 236, 2 Fam. L. Rev.
69, 1979 Cars­well­Ont 367 (Ont. C.A.), and
Kruger v. Kruger
(1980),
1979 CanLII 1663 (ON CA)
, 25
O.R. (2d) 673, 104 D.L.R. (3d) 481, 11 R.F.L. (2d) 52, 2 Fam. L. Rev. 197, 1979
Cars­well­Ont 299 (Ont. C.A.).  It is the sort of reservation to which a trial
court is ordinarily alive in an adjudication of a joint custody claim.

[
122
]

The court has not ruled out joint custody
altogether as an option for a child in situations of parental conflict.  Joint
custody within a parallel parenting plan may be used, if used carefully, to
address concerns of parental alienation.  See, for example,
Cox v. Down
(Stephen)
(2002),
2002 CanLII 78080 (ON SC)
, 30 R.F.L. (5th) 54, [2002] O.T.C. 499, [2002] O.J. No.
2762, 2002 Cars­well­Ont 2321 (Ont. S.C.),
per
Justice Lynda C.
Templeton; affirmed at
Cox
v. Down (Stephen)
(2003),
2003 CanLII 18571 (ON CA)
, 179 O.A.C. 45, 47 R.F.L. (5th) 1, [2003] O.J.
No. 4371, 2003 Cars­well­Ont 4554 (Ont. C.A.).  And indeed, trial courts have continued to make joint custody
orders within the context of appellate guidance, when a child’s best interests
call for that option, and consistent with a trial court’s duty to adjudicate
competing custody claims in a manner that is likely to serve the child’s best
interests.  See, for example,
Mol v. Mol

(1997), 40 O.T.C. 1, [1997]
O.J. No. 4060
, 1997 Cars­well­Ont 3693 (Ont. Gen Div.),
per
Justice
Emile R. Kruzick;
Dagg v. Pereira
(2000),
2000 CanLII 22459 (ON SC)
, 12 R.F.L. (5th) 325, [2000]
O.J. No. 4450, 2000 Cars­well­Ont 4390 (Ont. S.C.),
per
Justice Denise
E. Bellamy;
T.J.M. v. P.G.M.
(2002),
2002 CanLII 49550 (ON SC)
, 25 R.F.L. (5th) 78, [2002] O.J.
No. 398, 2002 Cars­well­Ont 356 (Ont. S.C.),
per
David R. Aston;
Anderson
v. Wilkins

(2002), 115 A.C.W.S. (3d) 96, [2002] O.J. No. 2724
, 2002 Cars­well­Ont
2233 (Ont. Fam. Ct.),
per
Justice Henry Vogelsang;
South v.
Tichelaar
(2001),
2001 CanLII 28133 (ON SC)
, 20 R.F.L. (5th) 175, [2001] O.J. No. 2823, 2001 Cars­well­Ont
2447 (Ont. S.C.),
per
Justice Thomas A. Heeney;
Sellick v. Bollert

(2004),
2004 CanLII 18894 (ON SC)
, 130 A.C.W.S. (3d) 1164, [2004] O.J. No. 2022, 2004 Cars­well­Ont 1934
(Ont. Fam. Ct.),
per
Justice Grant A. Campbell.  It is in essence an
option chosen by the trial court when it concludes that it is not in the child’s
best interests to entrust the primary caregiver with sole decision-making
power.

[
123
]

As I read the appellate jurisprudence on
joint custody, the essential concern is that trial judges not veer outside the
“best interests of the child” requirement of the legislation and into the use
of a joint custody either to “reward” one parent or to “punish” the other.  It
is also a concern that trial judges not fall prey to a “tunnel vision” on one
factor to the exclusion of other factors bearing on a child’s best interests;
that they not lose sight of the impact of a detailed parenting plan on
day-to-day life of the child; and that they not  overestimate the ability of
parents to make change in themselves.  The jurisprudence provides no “one size
fits all” approach to joint custody, nor would I expect that, if courts are to
be faithful to the statutory scheme for custody adjudications.

[
124
]

I do not read the appellate jurisprudence to
give licence to one parent deliberately to choreograph and then to perform a
dance about non-co-operation with the other parent in the expectation that the
nature, the source and the impetus for ongoing conflict will go unexplored.
Nor would that make sense.  To ignore the impact on a child of a parent who
deliberately fans conflict in the face of the other parent’s attempts to put it
to rest is to condone mischief.

[
125
]

Where, as here, the parent seeking joint
custody has been the “access” parent until now, a court pays particular
attention to the following factors:

(1)    The strength of this
child’s bond with his father — whether they have laid down a sufficient
familiarity with each other to attract this child’s respect for his father’s
guidance and care.

(2)    Risks, if any, presented
by this father.

(3)    Whether the plan for the
child’s parenting within the joint custody arrangement is centred in the
child’s needs and is likely to be reasonably managed by this child with the
support of each parent.

(4)    The father’s ability to
support this child’s relationship with his primary caregiver.

(5)    This father’s motivation
to work co-operatively with the child’s mother and her family.

4.12(a):   On the Child’s Relationship with His Father

[
126
]

A court might expect after such tough
sledding for a child and father in maintaining their relationship that there
would not be much of a relationship.  The evidence as a whole yields the
finding, contrary to the mother’s assertion, that this is more than a
“playmate” relationship and more than the sort of interaction that a child has
with any other friendly adult who pays attention to him.  This child has
managed to forge a strong bond with his father over the years.

[
127
]

The reports of the initial access centre
(exhibit 17), the report of the Office of the Children’s Lawyer and the
testimony of those other witnesses who have observed this child with his father
are powerful evidence of the bond that they have grown together.  The
development of that bond has been acknowledged and encouraged by the
ever-expanding access that the court has given this child over the course of this
litigation.  Mr. J.W. is “Daddy” in all the usual ways that a child recognizes
and responds to his male parent, a “Daddy” who has a solid place in this
child’s life despite his mother’s unhappiness about having the father there.

[
128
]

As a matter of common sense, it is not the
intensity of bond that the child has laid down with those in the maternal
family to whom he looks for his primary care, nor does the father expect it to
be that.  That does not make it less valuable to the child, nor less prized by
the father.

[
129
]

That the bond has been sustained is
testament to the commitment of the father to work through the resistance of the
mother, his skill in gaining the child’s trust, notwithstanding the mother’s
lack of support, and the child’s interest in time with his father.

[
130
]

The evidence as a whole does not support the
stance taken by the mother and maternal grandfather that M.P.R.W.’s difficult
behaviour after he returns from access are a sign that access is traumatic to
him because of his father’s parenting of him.  I considered the statements
allegedly made by M.P.R.W. to his mother about aspects of his father’s
parenting of him.  They did not rise above the level of allegation.  There was
no credible evidence to support a finding that the child made them in the form
conveyed by the mother and there is no ability to assess their reliability, if
they were made.

[
131
]

On the whole of the evidence related to his
time with his father, M.P.R.W. presents no significant problems to his father.
When he is with his father and his father’s family, he exhibits none of the
serious behaviour problems that he visits on his mother.  The father guides
what needs to be guided, refuses to be swept into the child’s attempts to tell
tales on his mother, responds sensibly to the child’s questions about the past
and his involvement in it.  The guidance is clear.  The ability to respond to
the child’s needs has been demonstrated to an array of responsible individuals
who have observed child and father together.  M.P.R.W. is valued but not
indulged in his father’s care.  This boy and his father can manage each other
in a responsible fashion.

4.12(b):  On the Issue of Risk to the Child in His
Father’s Care

[
132
]

At the age of three months, this child was
at risk for a brief time in his father’s care.

[
133
]

There is no present risk, nor is there
justification for a finding that this father poses a future risk to this boy.

[
134
]

This is not a case where the father denies
or minimizes the risk in which he placed his infant son.  He took his conduct
seriously.  He did not try to excuse it or to deflect responsibility for it.
He also frankly admitted that the mother had reason to be worried about the
baby at the time.  Although he did not immediately tell the mother what had
happened when she returned from her errand, he told her shortly thereafter when
it became apparent to him that the brief shaking may have caused some harm.  He
accompanied her and the child to the Hospital for Sick Children, remained
available and co-operative throughout the medical investigation, and throughout
the investigation by both police and the child protection authorities.  The
incident gave this father a good scare and keen insight into the duty of a
parent to be particularly careful that exhaustion or frustration does not get
in the way of a child’s need for safety.

[
135
]

The mother’s evidence on this voluntary
service agreement left the impression that the agreement centred solely on the
father’s need for intervention.  A plain read of the agreement indicates
otherwise.  Within the nine conditions of the agreement were terms that
both

parents allow the society social worker and high-risk nurse into the home on
both a scheduled and an unscheduled basis, that
both
parents were
to participate in parenting courses, that
both
parents were to
allow the public health nurse into the home, that
both
parents
were to participate in couple counselling.
Both
parents were to
sign consents on an as-needed basis by the society.  Thr father was to take an
anger management course, and not be left alone with the infant.  The mother was
to follow up on all M.P.R.W.’s medical needs.  The logical inference from that
agreement is that the society, quite sensibly, was responding not just to the
shaking episode itself, but to the stresses in the home that had contributed to
the father’s lapse in control.

[
136
]

The father completed the anger management
course.  He complied with the condition that he not be left alone with the
baby.  He waited for the society to re-evaluate him at the conclusion of the
voluntary service agreement.  No one from the society ever contacted him again.

[
137
]

This father took responsible steps to
moderate his conduct in an effort to shield his child from any future harm.  He
has succeeded in his efforts.

[
138
]

It was common ground (exhibit 1) that the
father has had only one parenting course in M.P.R.W.’s life to date — in
October 1999.  The mother devoted considerable time in the trial to her own
perception that he needs “refresher” courses.  I considered that.

[
139
]

Formal courses are not the only way in which
one equips oneself for responsible parenting.  Each child has his own unique
personality.  So does each parent.  Good parenting emerges from the growing
ability, achieved through a close and nurturing contact, to read and respond in
a timely fashion to the child’s cues. In short, one learns to parent by
parenting.  The father knows that.  There are also ways other than through
formal parenting courses to keep pace with an ever developing child — books,
television, videos and responsible adults within his family and circle of
friends to provide advice to him.

[
140
]

There is no justification for a finding that
this father requires formal parenting courses to inform his care of his son.

4.12(c):   On the Child-Centredness of the Joint Custody
Plan

[
141
]

This plan supports a continuation of the
child’s primary care by his mother and maternal grandparents.  It leaves intact
the routines to which he has become accustomed in his grandparents’ residence —
familiarity of place, familiarity of those in the maternal family who attend to
his day to day needs and the ease of contact with other maternal extended
family.

[
142
]

The plan also gives the child opportunity
for day care and schooling within a community with which he is already familiar
and the opportunity to grow friendships in that community, whether in his
neighbourhood or through actitivies in which the mother might wish to enroll
him during the time that he is in her care.

[
143
]

In relation to religious faith, this child
has both a Jewish and a Christian heritage.  Mr. J.W. is quite content that
M.P.R.W. be raised in the Jewish faith, as desired by the mother and her
family, and is prepared to support the child in that endeavour, provided it is
not used to deprive the child of opportunity to participate in the major
Christian holidays (Christmas and Easter) celebrated by the father and his
family.  He is prepared to share the child’s time when the Jewish and Christian
holidays overlap.  He looks to the mother for the same sharing.

[
144
]

He does not ask that this child, in the name
of joint custody, swing between their two households during the school week, or
that he have the child in his care every weekend.  His proposal for his own
parenting time with M.P.R.W. is modest and essentially builds incrementally on
what is presently in place for M.P.R.W.

[
145
]

There is reason to find the father sincere
in his respect for the rootedness that M.P.R.W. has laid down.  He has never
disputed the fact that, as between the two parents, he has not M.P.R.W.’s
primary caregiver.  This father has never sought to remove this child from the
primary care of his mother.  He has long respected the child’s bonds of
affection with her and her family.

4,12(d):  This Father’s Ability to Support the Child’s
Relationship with His Mother

[
146
]

On the whole of the trial evidence, Mr. J.W.
has shown a fine ability and motivation to support this child’s love of his
mother and her family.  That has included, most recently, managing M.P.R.W.’s
desire to stay longer in his father’s care by the clear message that their time
together is now ending, that they will see each other again soon and that his
mother is waiting for him.  That is precisely the direction needed for a little
boy.

4.12(e):   This Father’s Ability to Work Co-operatively
with the Child’s Mother

[
147
]

This is not a case where the father has laid
down a history of carping away at the mother’s care of their child.  It was his
evidence that Ms. A.Z. is a good mother in many ways.

[
148
]

This father has stood ready from the
earliest stages of this case to work co-operatively with this mother.  He has
sought, quite reasonably, the measure of co-operation from the mother and her
family needed to enable this boy to have a strong and nurturing relationship
with him.

[
149
]

He has been generous and flexible with the
mother in access arrangements, when there has been reason in the child’s
interest to do that.  He has also foregone access himself when it was in the
child’s interests to do that.  He declined to take the child for access during
the weekend of the summer 2003 Toronto blackout, for example, because he did not want to expose the child
to public transportation that might shut down without notice.  That was a
sensible and child-centred decision.

[
150
]

Where he has resisted the desires of the
mother, his resistance has been rooted in his perception, grounded by the
evidence in this trial, that she is deliberately attempting to withhold the
child from access or otherwise diminish the child’s relationship with him.  On
the whole of the evidence relevant to that resistance, he would have failed
M.P.R.W., had he not tried so hard to protect the child’s opportunity to have
his father in his life.

4.13:   On the Impact of This Father’s Financial
Precariousness

[
151
]

For reasons separately released on 13 July
2004, I did not find that the father has deliberately ignored his financial
obligations to this child, deliberately misstated or hidden income or that he
has acted in a manner designed to provide as little as possible for this child,
as Ms. A.Z. had argued.

[
152
]

There were arrears in child support at the
close of the trial.  I considered that.  The father is not trying to shy away
from that indebtedness. He had negotiated an arrears payment schedule with the
Family Responsibility Office (exhibit 22).

[
153
]

It is true that Mr. J.W. has had the benefit
of a number of downward variations of this child support payments.  On the
whole of the trial evidence, the interim variations from time to time were
amply justified when set in the context of the father’s steadily deteriorating
financial health.

[
154
]

I have taken into account that the father
needs to lay down within his own household the sorts of supplies needed by an
almost five-year-old vhild during his times with his father, including a modest
supply of clothing, so that the mother is not feeling that she needs to send
the child with an array of supplies for his weekends with his father.  I am
confident that the father, with the assistance of his family, has the ability
to provide what is needed.  It is not necessary for the child to have a full
set of outer clothing or footwear in both homes.

4.14:   On the Father’s Attention to the Child’s
Relationships with Paternal Extended Family

[
155
]

Ms. A.Z. is right that the extended paternal
family does not know this child well at this point in his life, and that there
has been relatively sparse contact for the child with its members.

[
156
]

The mother has also played a role in
constraining the child’s ability to have that contact.  The gap in contact with
the father was also a gap in contact with any member of his family.  The mother
initially resisted the inclusion of extended family in the supervised access
visits, necessitating an order of the court to pave the way for that
inclusion.  For Aunt H.W., for example, it was some 18 months post-parental
separation before she again saw her nephew.  I have dealt with the scuttling of
a birthday visit with Aunt H.W. elsewhere in these reasons.

[
157
]

The father has done his best in difficult
circumstances to keep alive for this child a measure of relationship with his
extended paternal family.  The members of the extended family have their residences
and workplaces some considerable distance from Toronto.  Aunt H.W., for example, has been able to easily co-ordinate her
own work schedules with the father’s access weekends.

4.15:   On the Ability of These Parents to Manage
Communication with Each Other

[
158
]

There is no question that joint custody in
high conflict circumstances has the potential to cause real mischief for a
child where parents are so invested in their warfare with each other that they
blind themselves to the impact of their conduct on their child’s wellbeing.

[
159
]

This case is not a situation of “high
conflict”, on the whole of the evidence relevant to conflict in this case and
unlike the evidence in
Johnson
v. Cleroux
,
supra
, that suggested to the Ontario Court of Appeal
continuing conflict around parenting issues.  The father does not seek to
impose his parenting style on the mother.  This is not a father with a “starkly
incompatible approach and wish for child rearing that causes the child to
suffer from being caught between antagonistic forces and pressure”, as in, for
example,
Kappler v. Beaudoin
(2000),
2000 CanLII 22579 (ON SC)
, 6 R.F.L. (5th) 269, [2000] O.T.C.
302, [2000] O.J. No. 1558, 2000 Cars­well­Ont 1636 (Ont. Fam. Ct.).  This father
has no desire for conflict with this mother.

[
160
]

In looking at the level of co-operation that
has been demonstrated over the course of this litigation, I paid particular
attention to the various interim agreements that formed part of the trial
evidence.  Ms. A.Z. also wanted me to regard offers to settle.  That I declined
to do.  As a matter of procedural law governing the case, offers to settle come
before the court within an adjudication of what costs, if any, are to be borne
by either party.

[
161
]

This case is “high conflict” only if
deference is given to the mother to keep conflict alive in this child’s life.
A court required to serve the best interests of the child cannot give that deference
to this mother.  This is not a case where the mother in constitutionally unable
to alter her behaviour.

[
162
]

Courts charged with such a heavy
responsibility to a child do not set about to create mischief by over-rating
the abilities of parents to manage a joint custody order.  M.P.R.W. is blessed
with intelligent, caring parents, who have been lost far too long in litigation.
This father has been seeking co-operation from the mother throughout this
case.  This mother has the ability, when motivated, to meet directly with this
father to try to resolve matters respecting their son.  She is also able to see
the benefits of cooperation for M.P.R.W.  On 9 June 2002 when these parents signed their
temporary agreement, Ms. A.Z. testified to M.P.R.W.’s response:“ M.P.R.W. was
very happy about seeing this, he had never seen this kind of peace between his
parents.”

[
163
]

It is time for these parents to give
M.P.R.W. peace between his parents.

4.16:   On the Father’s Case for a Mobility Restriction

[
164
]

Claims for restrictions on a custodial
parent’s mobility are decided within the context of a child’s best interests,
as any other incident of custody.  In the context of sole custody orders, the
parent entrusted with that responsibility is owed a high measure of deference.

[
165
]

Mr. J.W. seeks an order restricting any
relocation of the child’s primary residence to a 30-kilometre radius of Toronto without his written consent or
alternatively, an order of the court.  Mr. J.W.’s concern is that the mother
will set out to dwindle the child’s relationship with him by relocating to a
place too far away for a regularly scheduled contact.

[
166
]

Ms. A.Z. testified that it would be “unfair”
to place any restriction on her at all, “since [she] was the parent responsible
for all the child’s needs and interests.”  Then in her closing submissions, she
proposed an order allowing her freedom to relocate within 200 kilometres of Toronto.

[
167
]

Although she had testified that she expected
to reside with her parents for the next few years until she reduced her debt
load, she also made it quite clear that she would go wherever lucrative employment
and good schools beckoned, so that she could provide the standard of life for
herself and this boy that she desires for them — whether northern Ontario, the
outskirts of the Greater Toronto Area or the United States.  She saw no
significant impact on the child — certainly no loss of his maternal family
relationships.  She would manage the child’s access, if in northern Ontario, for example, by trekking him by
bus to and from Toronto — a
proposal that had no ring of truth to it in light of the difficulties that she
has thrown in the way of this child’s relationship with his father.  It became
increasingly uncertain what she would do and how she would weigh the impact of
her desired relocation, wherever it might be, on the child.

[
168
]

The whole of the trial evidence bearing on
her management of her interim custody responsibility justifies a shield for
this child from an impulsive and self-centred uprooting, given the ease with
which a relocation of the child can be used as a tool to place the child
outside of the reach of the father’s financial ability to sustain contact with
their son.

[
169
]

The mother points out that it is the
quality, not the quantity, of access that matters.  Quality is important, to be
sure.  M.P.R.W. has that already.  As a matter of common sense and human
experience, it is the regularity of contact, as well as the quality of contact,
that is the key to growing a relationship that has been thwarted in so many
ways so many times by her attitude.  M.P.R.W. is still very young.  Continuity
of contact is critical for him.  He needs to have both parents actively
involved in this child’s life to offset the likelihood that he will be
swallowed up in his mother’s needs and desires.

[
170
]

A mobility restriction is needed by this
child, but his best interests are not served by the mobility restriction
proposed by either parent.

[
171
]

It is makes common sense to focus on what is
reasonable travel time between each parent’s household, taking into account the
child’s age and ability to manage long-distance travel and the mode of
transportation.  M.P.R.W. needs his parents residing within reasonable travel
time of each other.  His father relies on public transit, unless extended
family offer an alternative from time to time.  His mother, but for the
transportation assistance provided by her parents, is also dependent on public
transit.  Taxi transport is an extraordinary expense for either parent at this
time in their economic life.

[
172
]

It is for these reasons that I have tied the
mobility to travel time and for a specified period.  As a matter of common
sense, the older the child, the better his ability to cope with longer distance
travel.

5:     CREDIBILITY FINDINGS

5.1:     The Mother

[
173
]

Ms. A.Z. impressed this court as a bright
and articulate woman, very personable, meticulous in her attention to things
that matter to her.  Her tenacity is both a blessing to fuel her quest for
further accomplishments in her life and a curse in relation to her motivation
to hear voices other than her own on matters affecting this child.  To a large
extent, this litigation has been kept alive for so long because of that
inability.

[
174
]

I took into account throughout the trial and
in my deliberations that Ms. A.Z. was not represented by counsel at trial,
although it appeared on her evidence that she had had counsel at various stages
of the litigation.  There were times in the trial that she required firm
direction.  Her anxiety gets seriously in the way of her motivation to abide
direction.

[
175
]

This mother’s case suffered considerably
from her inability to see the perspective of anyone other than her own.
“Fairness” in her eyes is what suited her needs, irrespective of the impact on
anyone else.  Indeed, having used up the bulk of the trial time scheduled for
the case to put in her own case, and with more time needed, she indicated on 15
March 2004 that she would greatly appreciate it if the court could finish the
case “this week” because she had a job offer waiting for her when the trial was
over — working as a paralegal for paralegal firm doing business in the Small Claims
Court.  She appeared oblivious to the fact that her manner of conducting her
case was the root cause of the trial taking “a considerable amount of time”.
She appeared equally oblivious that the court had a duty to receive the case
presented by the father.

[
176
]

Although she made numerous reference in the
course of the trial to her “learning disability”, she presented no evidence of
any disability, and I found none.  Her problems in recalling names and dates
from times now past were the ordinary problems encountered by witnesses who are
suddenly called upon to remember facts that had no particular significance at
the time.  Her inability to recall the names of assessors now scheduled to
enter the life of this child was more concerning but, in the end, I did not
conclude that she was deliberately attempting to withhold that particular
information from the court.

[
177
]

Although she would invite this court to find
that the father was the one who had stripped her of her confidence to manage
the aftermath of the parental separation, the trial evidence does not justify
that finding.  On the whole of the trial evidence and her demeanour in the
courtroom, Ms. A.Z. appears dependent by nature, quite immature in her own
emotional development, with sensibilities and sensitivities that appear to be
nurtured both by her and her father.

[
178
]

Although the evidence of the mother on the
child’s experience in her care was not significantly contradicted in the trial,
her desire that the court rest its findings about the child solely on her own
experience of him and, to a lesser extent, on the experience of the maternal
grandfather, notwithstanding clear indication that others in the community had
relevant information about him drawn from their own substantial involvement
with him, left this court very wary of the reliability of her evidence,
particularly when that evidence was set against the starkly different picture
of this child that emerged from the evidence of the father and his witnesses
and the maternal grandmother, ultimately found more credible.

[
179
]

Her decisions about what was to be placed
before this court’s eyes for decision-making invited the inference that she was
deliberately attempting to withhold from the court information bearing on this
child’s best interests and to deflect attention more towards her accusations
about the father.  This court had no evidence, for example, from the child’s
day-care providers with which to evaluate whether the mother’s experience of
this child is also their own.  According to the uncontradicted evidence of the
mother, M.P.R.W. has been in day care from early morning to late in the
afternoon for five days of the week over the course of the last 18 months and
that evidence could have been of considerable assistance in establishing the
reliability of the mother’s own evidence.

[
180
]

Her perceptions of lags and other
difficulties in this boy’s development were also not supported by any evidence
independent of her.  For example, whether the goals of the Hincks-Dellcrest
clinical intervention were met from the perception of the clinician remained an
unknown at the close of trial.  The mother produced no evidence from the
counsellor, taking the stance that “ it was to benefit us, it wasn’t for
purpose of court”.  She displayed a real reluctance to provide any meaningful
information about these interventions.  Although her brother is a developmental
paediatrician, according to her evidence, and presumably could have provided a
reliable indicator of the extent, if at all, to which M.P.R.W. is lagging in
his development, no evidence on that point was provided by him.  In light of
the evidence of the mother and maternal grandfather that there is a strong
familial bond in this family and that they all serve as an important support
network for this child, I was surprised that this evidence was not forthcoming.

[
181
]

She was quick to act on assumptions and
belief without taking the time to explore whether her assumption and belief has
any reasonable basis.  She was quick to float innuendo.  For example, although
she acknowledged that the father had no direct contact with her in the period
from 8 to 30 January 2001, she leapt to the belief that a complaint by
“somebody on behalf of the father” to the children’s aid society with some
“very serious allegations” that she was not feeding her son, that she was
keeping him dirty and drugging him to get him to sleep was “indirect
harassment”.  Her response was to call the police “because he wasn’t supposed
to be bothering us”, and “it was clear by what was said by Children’s Aid that
he was trying to cause trouble for us,  . . .  trying to cause me to
lose my child”.  She would have this court believe that the family apartment
was in such disarray and dirt that it took her four days to “get it back to
liveable condition”, suggesting by inference that the father had trashed it.
On another occasion, “somebody” had fed M.P.R.W. something before he was ready
for it and he got hives — an event that happened “right at the end of the
relationship”.  I found no truth in any of these assumptions.

[
182
]

She focused her case essentially on an
attempt to portray this father as an abuser and deadbeat and herself and the
child a victim of his controlling behaviour.  In doing that she rested secure
in her belief that a court would find her and her evidence believable.  That
did not happen.

5.2:     The Father

[
183
]

As between the two parents, the father
emerged as the more credible witness.  His case was measured, child-centred
throughout and generous to the mother.  I found no hyperbole, no rush to
judgment, no attempt to denigrate this mother or her family.  He responded
frankly to the questions asked of him, whether posed by his own counsel, Ms.
A.Z. or the court.  He kept his calm in the face of demeaning comment visited
on him by both the mother and the maternal grandfather, appearing more saddened
than angered by their disrespect of him.

[
184
]

He impressed this court as a modest man,
with a strong work ethic, a tenacity and patience that has been tested acutely
over very draining years in his life.  He is very aware of his place on the
economic ladder in comparison with the place enjoyed by the maternal family.
In the eyes of this court, his fewer material resources did not make him any
less a valuable father for this boy.

[
185
]

He has succeeded in his case in large part
because he has shown himself to be the more thoughtful and mature parent,
better able to set aside his own needs and interests when the child’s needs
require him to do that.

5.3:     The Maternal Grandfather

[
186
]

The maternal grandfather assisted his
daughter throughout the trial and did so in a careful fashion.  I was also
impressed with his ability to hear the court’s concerns when his daughter
appeared to deafen herself and to act on them.  He has a sincere interest in
the well being of this grandson and that was evident throughout the trial.

[
187
]

I found the maternal grandfather too tightly
aligned with his daughter’s perceptions of her life with Mr. J.W., for reasons
that made no common sense on the whole of the evidence and, at the close of the
trial, there was no rational explanation for his failure to see the impact of
his daughter’s frailties on the wellbeing of this child.

5.4:     Other Witnesses

[
188
]

I found the other witnesses in the trial
credible and accepted their evidence as a reliable indication of their
experience and observations.

6:     CONCLUSION

[
189
]

For all of the foregoing reasons, it is the
conclusion of this court that it is likely contrary to this child’s best
interests, in both the short and for the foreseeable long term, to entrust
solely to the mother’s decision-making, both the rights and the
responsibilities embedded in a sole custody order.

[
190
]

At this time in his life and for the
foreseeable future, M.P.R.W. needs a calm and consistent support and periods of
less stressed parenting to offset his mother’s excesses.  The father’s proposal
for joint custody is the option likely to be better suited to meet this child’s
ongoing best interests.  The plan provides assurance to this child that his
father is recognized as an important decisionmaker, together with his mother,
in his life.  By removing from the mother the sole decision-making
responsibility, it ensures that proposals for this child that by their nature
cause disruption if implemented, including health care and education decisions,
are not taken to feed the mother’s needs and whims, but centred on the needs
and benefits to the child.

Vacation

in the summer of 2005 and until the summer of 2007, and subject to his father’s

in the summer of 2009 and thereafter each summer, the child is to be in his

(i)    The
child is to have his own passport, and each parent is to sign whatever

(ii)    The
original passport is to be held by the father and delivered on request to the

(iii)    For
any out-of-province travel with the child, each parent will provide the other

(i)    Telephone
Access:  Each parent is to provide the child with reasonable opportunity to
make telephone contact with the other parent, if the child expresses a desire

(j)    Unexpected
Changes to the Parenting Schedule:  In the event of illness or other unexpected

Sharing

(i)    Each
parent is to have equal and direct access to all information bearing on the

later than 15 August 2004, the mother is to provide the father with a list of

parent is to do what is needed to enable an easy and effective flow of

parents are to keep each other current on any change in their address or

(i)    When

parent is to make it consistently clear to the child that he is to respect the

(v)    To
the best of their ability, and they are each to call forth the best within

their attention on what is likely to serve the child’s best interests at the
age and stage in his development that any particular decision must be made.

they are unable to reach consensus on any particular decision, authority for

upbringing: the mother

the father

health and dental care: the father
